words.etymon: pie-lex-gwemtus gʷémtus (mis-mapped; elsewhere in slab h₂wéh₁n̥ts)

cognate: Lat. uīs = Gk ἴς (*wiH-s 'force'), exact cognate head noun; both are old root nouns, and Gk ἴς is archaic and nearly confined to formulae
drift_or_renewal: renewal of the dependent: Lat. uentus (*h₂weh₁-nt-) for Gk ἄνεμος (*h₂enh₁-mo-). The exact cognate of ἄνεμος, Lat. animus/anima, also stands with uis in Lucretius (uis animi/animai, e.g. lat:LucrDRN3 3.499 in B-50c42) but has drifted from 'wind/breath' to 'mind/soul': the old pair survives with the dependent's meaning shifted, while the 'wind' sense is carried by the renewed uentus
shared_syntax: nominative 'force' noun + adnominal genitive of the wind, the phrase standing as agent subject of a verb of violent motion (Lat. uerberat, ruit, uerrit, perscindat; Gk διέσχισεν, ἀπώσατο, κατήγαγεν, ὀφέλλει, ἐπιβρέμει)
context: storm wind as a destructive agent at sea and against ships: Lucr. 1.271 'uenti uis uerberat ... pontum' + 'ruit nauis'; 5.1226 'uis ... per mare uenti' sweeping a fleet; Od. 9.71 'διέσχισεν ἲς ἀνέμοιο' (sails torn); Od. 13.276/19.186 the force of the wind drives sailors off course; Il. 15.383 'ἲς ἀνέμου' that swells the waves; Hes. Op. 518 'ἲς ἀνέμου Βορέου'
phrase: *wiHs + gen. 'wind' = 'the force of the wind' as an agent: uenti uis ~ ἲς ἀνέμοιο
note: Against inheritance: both languages build 'force of X' freely (ἲς ποταμοῖο, ἲς Ἠελίου; uis Solis, uis ignis, uis amnis), and all Latin witnesses are Lucretius writing physics, 24 sentences in all, of which about 14 are the real genitive phrase. For inheritance: the archaic ἴς is restricted to fixed phrases, and the wind is its most frequent genitive (5 times in Homer, plus Hesiod), in the same storm-at-sea context as Lucretius. Do not use Hes. Th. 951 'ἲς Ἡρακλῆος' as a witness: that is the personal periphrasis type (ἱερὴ ἲς Τηλεμάχοιο).

cognate: Lat. sōl ~ Ved. sū́rya- (*sóh₂wl̥ / derivative); Lat. serpēns = Ved. sárpant- (thematic present participle of *sérp-e-, morphologically exact)
drift_or_renewal: none (Ved. sūrya- is a derivative of the same noun); Gk ἕρπω has generalised to 'go' and is not attested with the sun in the local corpora
shared_syntax: 'sun' + present participle of *serp- agreeing with it, the participle describing the sun's own motion
context: the sun's progress across the sky: Lucretius, the sun creeping through the zodiac and closing the year's seasons ('sol ... serpens'); AV 4.20.7, 'like the sun creeping in the clear sky' (vīdhre 'in the clear sky', simile)
note: For: both words are exact cognates in the same construction, and the collocation is rare on both sides (sṛp with the sun: twice in AV, none in RV; serpo with the sun: once in the Latin corpus; ἕρπω with ἥλιος: none in Greek). Against: each side has a single witness, and 'the slowly creeping sun' is a natural image that could have arisen independently.

cognate: Lat. superus ~ Av. upara- (*(s)upero-); Lat. inferus ~ Av. aδara- (*n̥dʰero-)
drift_or_renewal: Vedic renews the 'upper' member (úttara- … ádhara-, e.g. RV 1.32.9, 10.42.11); Ved. úpara- has drifted to 'lower/later'
shared_syntax: antonymic pair of *-ero- comparatives forming a polar merism (upper ones / lower ones = all of them)
context: Pl. Aul. 368 'superi ... inferi' (those above / those below, punning on gods above and below); Yt (CAB 'YtMihr30.5') 'aδara dāta ... upara dāta' (the lower and the upper creations, = all creation)
phrase: *upero- / *n̥dʰero- 'upper and lower' as a merism of totality
note: The contexts do not match (a Plautine joke against Avestan liturgy), and a polar 'above/below' pair is close to universal. This mainly shows that the antonym pair was inherited, not that a phrase was.

All 249 Latin-pivot bundles read. Most are shared-root noise (Lucretian 'uis animi' ~ AV vayas/prāṇa, ORu Church Slavonic 'въ вѣкы' calques, Hippocratic prose). Three claims: uis uenti ~ ἲς ἀνέμοιο (medium); sol serpens ~ sūryam sarpantam (low); superi/inferi ~ upara/aδara merism (low). Rejected: ulcus alendo ~ ἕλκε' ἀπαλθήσεσθον (senses opposite), domos/tigna ~ δῶμα/στέγη (generic).
